top_rules: Never reference Project or call Task.getProject() inside a task action — grep for getProject()/.project. inside doLast/doFirst bodies.
Never enumerate System.getenv()/getProperties() without a filter — use providers.environmentVariablesPrefixedBy() or a named getenv('KEY') lookup.
Never read a file directly at configuration time — use providers.fileContents(...).asText.
Never shell out (ProcessBuilder/Runtime.exec/ExecOperations.exec) at configuration time — use providers.exec()/ValueSource.
Never register a BuildListener/TaskExecutionListener from a plugin — use a Build Service via BuildEventsListenerRegistry; still-open gradle/gradle#18520 proves this is live friction.
CI must run with --configuration-cache and triage the report, not blanket-suppress with warn mode — Gradle 9 made warn mode discard incompatible-task cache entries anyway.
When migrating, audit third-party plugins first, not your own tasks — Square's 2022 postmortem's only two blockers were Anvil and Wire, not application code.
Treat Isolated Projects as diagnostics-only, not a CI gate — incubating only since 9.7.0 (2026-08-06), with cross-build and build-to-project constraints explicitly not fully enforced yet.
surprises: gradle/gradle#24040: Gradle 9 changed maven-publish behavior so explicit repository credentials now silently DISABLE the configuration cache for that task instead of failing the build — a build can look fully successful while quietly never being cached.

The prior audit (exemplar-build-shape.md) itself asserts 'Gradle 9's default is already on regardless of the property,' which the primary sources (9.0.0 release notes, the road-to-configuration-cache blog) directly contradict — it's preferred-with-automatic-fallback, default still targeted at Gradle 11, not on by default in 9.x.

org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects isn't just an old alias floating in blogs — the 9.7.0 release notes formally deprecate it in that release, with 0/32 exemplars using it versus 5/32 on the live org.gradle.isolated-projects key.

Isolated Projects' own 9.7.0 docs admit two of four constraint categories (cross-build access, build-to-project access) are 'not fully enforced yet' — the feature can't yet catch everything it claims to forbid.

gradle/gradle#18520 (build-listener ban has no full replacement API for build-start/build-finish hooks, only task-completion) is still open years after the documented fix pattern existed — the 'documented replacement' isn't actually complete for every BuildListener use case.

The reviewer's compliance check has no dedicated task — it's just the real build/test command plus --configuration-cache, and 'clean' is the ABSENCE of a problems-summary line and HTML report, not a positive success signal from any task.

top_rules: SHOULD (not MUST) prefer included build-logic over buildSrc — 9/32 flagships (spring-boot, dagger, kotlinx.coroutines...) still use buildSrc; never call it a defect.
Any Settings plugin in build-logic MUST live in a separate minimal included build (build-logic-settings), never folded into the ordinary convention-plugin module, once that module exists.
Never write dot-notation catalog accessors (libs.guava) inside a precompiled script plugin — they are not generated there and never compile, in any Gradle version through 9.x.
Inside build-logic, read catalog coordinates via extensions.getByType<VersionCatalogsExtension>().named("libs").findLibrary/findVersion/findPlugin — the officially sanctioned workaround.
Never use the internal org.gradle.accessors.dm.LibrariesForLibs reflection hack — unsupported, breaks across Gradle versions and in buildSrc/test.
A plugin consumed via alias(libs.plugins.x) cannot be used inside a precompiled script plugin's plugins{} block at all — declare it as a marker-artifact dependency and apply(plugin="id") instead.
buildSrc/settings.gradle.kts must explicitly re-import the version catalog via dependencyResolutionManagement{versionCatalogs{...}} before any catalog access works there.

The OCX Gradle plugin's own dev repo does not need build-logic-settings on day one (single module); it becomes a MUST only once that repo grows a second ordinary build-logic module while still needing an early Settings plugin.
surprises: gradle/gradle#15383 is still fully open after nearly 6 years with a maintainer stating the gap may be architecturally unfixable (precompiled plugins are compiled before the consuming catalog is known), not merely unprioritized.

The build-logic-settings split is not universal even among included-build adopters: junit-framework includes two ordinary modules together with no settings-only module, and jjohannes's reference repo mixes Settings and ordinary plugins in one module.

There is no workaround at all — supported or unsupported — for using alias(libs.plugins.x) inside a precompiled script plugin's plugins{} block, because that block is evaluated against a dummy project before any catalog exists.

dagger centralizes the string-keyed catalog workaround into a dedicated buildSrc helper file (VersionCatalogs.kt) rather than repeating it per convention plugin — a reusable pattern worth citing as the concrete fix.
Zero corpus repos at the measured SHAs use the internal LibrariesForLibs reflection hack — the supported VersionCatalogsExtension API is universal in the checked-out convention-plugin code.

top_rules: Every custom task/transform property MUST carry exactly one input/output/@Internal/@Console annotation — verify via validatePlugins reporting missing_annotation
Never annotate a File/Directory-typed property @Input; use @InputFile/@InputDirectory — validatePlugins catches it as incorrect_use_of_input_annotation
@PathSensitive(NONE) for single files, @PathSensitive(RELATIVE) for directories; ABSOLUTE breaks cross-machine cache relocatability — grep PathSensitivity.ABSOLUTE
A JVM compile classpath input MUST be @CompileClasspath, never @InputFiles/@Classpath — it enables ABI-level compile avoidance by ignoring everything but ABI-affecting class changes
Every cacheable task's file inputs need a normalization strategy or caching is 'highly ineffective' per Gradle's own docs (missing_normalization_annotation)
Task ordering must be wired via Provider/output chains, never inferred from a bare File reference plus incidental execution order (implicit_dependency)
CI must run './gradlew validatePlugins' as an explicit step — java-gradle-plugin registers the task on any module, plugin or not, so its existence proves nothing ran or failed

On Gradle ≥9.0.0 an explicit reproducibleFileOrder=false/preserveFileTimestamps=true/useFileSystemPermissions() block is an active reproducibility opt-out requiring a justifying comment — read the wrapper version before judging, never assume it's a harmless legacy no-op
surprises: Kafka's block (build.gradle:362-364) is not merely 'restates defaults' as the wave-1 audit's headline framed it — direct fetch of the Gradle 9.0.0 upgrade guide shows it's a byte-for-byte copy of Gradle's own documented 3-property 'revert to pre-9 archive behaviour' snippet (including useFileSystemPermissions()), applied on a repo pinned to wrapper 9.7.1: a total, deliberate-looking opt-out of reproducibility, most plausibly an unexamined pre-9 carry-over never revisited during the Gradle 8→9 upgrade.

Two of the three real (non-false-positive) reproducible-archive hits in the corpus (micronaut-core, spotless) are the OPPOSITE problem from kafka: they correctly set the pre-9 values for reproducibility, which is now simply dead code restating the Gradle 9 default — harmless, but a rule can't just say 'check these properties are set correctly', it has to branch on wrapper version.

validatePlugins and the java-gradle-plugin jar-time check are two independently-implemented validations that overlap in content but differ in severity: the jar-time check only ever warns (confirmed live on the current docs page), while validatePlugins fails the build by default (confirmed via its own javadoc) — an agent that sees a warning and calls it fine can miss a check that would hard-fail.

It could not be confirmed from any primary Gradle doc that validatePlugins is wired into check/build by default for a java-gradle-plugin module — community sources hedge with 'typically wired', so the safe normative rule is an explicit CI step, not reliance on implicit lifecycle wiring.

The gradle/gradle docs source path for the 31 validation-problem IDs lives under a directory literally named 'unused/' (platforms/documentation/docs/src/docs/userguide/unused/validation_problems.adoc) yet the page is live, current, and matches docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/validation_problems.html exactly — the directory name is a docs-build artifact, not a deprecation signal, worth flagging so nobody discounts the source.

GRADLE-CACHE-02 — Never read a file, spawn a process, or resolve a Configuration at configuration time; use providers.fileContents/providers.exec/ValueSource.
GRADLE-CACHE-03 — Never enumerate System.getenv()/getProperties(); name the key or use providers.environmentVariablesPrefixedBy.
GRADLE-CACHE-04 — Never register a BuildListener or TaskExecutionListener; use a Build Service via BuildEventsListenerRegistry.
GRADLE-CACHE-05 — Never hold live-JVM state (ClassLoader/Thread/Socket/locks) or Gradle/Settings/SourceSet/Configuration in task fields or inputs.
GRADLE-CACHE-06 — Enable the cache via org.gradle.configuration-cache=true in gradle.properties, not a CI-only flag, and leave problems mode at fail.
GRADLE-CACHE-07 — Gate a published Gradle plugin on a TestKit test asserting a --configuration-cache build with zero problems.
GRADLE-CACHE-08 — Never read a green build as a cached build; verify the second run prints 'Reusing configuration cache.'
GRADLE-CACHE-09 — Write org.gradle.isolated-projects, never org.gradle.unsafe.isolated-projects.
GRADLE-CACHE-10 — Run Isolated Projects in diagnostics mode only; never make it a required CI gate.
GRADLE-CACHE-11 — Give every task/transform property exactly one input/output/@Internal/@Console annotation.
GRADLE-CACHE-12 — Never annotate a File/RegularFileProperty/DirectoryProperty with @Input.
GRADLE-CACHE-13 — Declare normalization on every file input: NONE for a file, RELATIVE for a directory, never ABSOLUTE.
GRADLE-CACHE-14 — Annotate a JVM compile classpath @CompileClasspath, not @InputFiles or @Classpath.
GRADLE-CACHE-15 — Wire task-to-task dependencies through Provider/task-output chains, never a bare File plus dependsOn.
GRADLE-CACHE-16 — Run ./gradlew validatePlugins as an explicit CI step with enableStricterValidation = true for any published plugin.
GRADLE-CACHE-17 — On Gradle >=9.0.0 add no archive reproducibility properties, and treat any explicit setting as an opt-out needing a comment.
GRADLE-STRUCT-01 — Put new shared build logic in an included build-logic build; never call an existing buildSrc deprecated or a defect.
GRADLE-STRUCT-02 — Split Settings plugins into a separate minimal build-logic-settings included build when build-logic also holds ordinary convention plugins.
GRADLE-STRUCT-03 — Never use dot-notation catalog accessors in a precompiled script plugin; bind VersionCatalogsExtension.named(...) and use findLibrary/findVersion/findPlugin.
GRADLE-STRUCT-04 — Never import org.gradle.accessors.dm.LibrariesForLibs.
GRADLE-STRUCT-05 — Never write alias(libs.plugins.x) in a precompiled script plugin's plugins{} block; declare the marker artifact and apply by id.
GRADLE-STRUCT-06 — Re-declare the version catalog in buildSrc/settings.gradle.kts before any buildSrc catalog access.
GRADLE-STRUCT-07 — Express cross-cutting configuration as a convention plugin, not root-level allprojects{}/subprojects{}.
GRADLE-STRUCT-08 — Set rootProject.name explicitly in the root settings file.
GRADLE-STRUCT-09 — Add a module through whatever mechanism generates the module list; never append a literal include() beside a generator, never count include( lines.

Resolved for the dive (release notes normative over audit inference): apache__kafka@940c100fab:build.gradle:362-364 is an active, total reproducibility opt-out. Makes GRADLE-CACHE-17 version-gated rather than the usual 'add the block' advice.

Configuration cache 'on by default in Gradle 9': exemplar-build-shape.md's Contradictions section asserts it; the cc dive fetched the 9.0.0 release notes and road-to-configuration-cache and found preferred-with-automatic-fallback with the default targeted at Gradle 11. Resolved for the dive; the audit sentence is an overstatement, matching topic-map conflict 18.

build-logic-settings severity: the build-logic dive proposed MUST; its own Contested section then records junit-team__junit-framework@35c56a8e02:settings.gradle.kts:2-4 and jjohannes's reference repo shipping the merged form, with no stated size threshold anywhere. Resolved to SHOULD (GRADLE-STRUCT-02) — Gradle's wording is comparative ('A better solution'), the cost is caching throughput not correctness, and a MUST would flag JUnit and a Gradle Developer Advocate's teaching repo.

Must CI pass --configuration-cache? The cc dive's candidate #6 reads as yes; pub measured the flag in 3/32 workflows vs the property in 10/32. Resolved: gradle.properties is the canonical switch and the check reads it first (GRADLE-CACHE-06); a CLI flag is for overriding one job, and requiring it would flag nearly every adopter.

validatePlugins warns or fails? java_gradle_plugin.html documents a jar-time warning; the ValidatePlugins javadoc says the task fails by default. Resolved: two distinct gates at different times — the jar-time check warns, the task fails, and a plugin author who only runs `build` never hits the second. Hence GRADLE-CACHE-16 requires the explicit invocation.

Isolated Projects adoption (5/32) read as maturity: resolved against the 9.7.0 docs' own 'not fully enforced yet' on two of four constraint categories — adoption of the property is not adoption of a gate (GRADLE-CACHE-10), while the dead org.gradle.unsafe.* key stays a mechanical MUST (GRADLE-CACHE-09).
needs_another_round: maven-publish x configuration cache — is maven-publish fully cache-compatible on Gradle 9.7.x, partially (only the explicit-credentials path falls back per #24040), or still broadly incompatible? The cc dive fetched the issue and a March-2025 Gradle blog claim and could not resolve it; this blocks a precise GRADLE-CACHE-08 and touches GRADLE-PUB.

GRADLE-STRUCT rows never dived — M-B-05 (two subprojects sharing a leaf name causing wrong conflict resolution with no build failure, gradle/gradle#847) and M-B-07 (a subproject gradle.properties overriding root settings the configuration cache assumes fixed): both adjudicated P0/P1, neither covered by a wave-2 dive, both silent-failure shapes.

Remote build cache push-gating — 10 buildCache{} blocks across 6 repos but no checked-out settings file shows remote(HttpBuildCache){ isPush = ... }; 'who may push to the shared cache' is the one build-cache correctness question the corpus has not answered.

Gradle 10 archive defaults — GRADLE-CACHE-17 is framed 9-vs-8; nothing in the 9.0.0/9.7.0 notes says whether Gradle 10 changes archive reproducibility again. Re-check when Gradle 10's release notes exist.

top_rules: Never import a Gradle type from an internal-segment package or an *Internal/*Impl type — Gradle can break these in any release including minors.
Never assume another plugin is applied; use pluginManager.apply(id) for hard deps or pluginManager.withPlugin(id) {} for optional integration.
Ban afterEvaluate except fail-fast validation of your own plugin's state; replace with lazy Property/Provider wiring, convention() defaults, and pluginManager.withPlugin().
Annotate every task property and run validatePlugins explicitly in CI — the built-in jar-time check only warns, never fails.
Choose the reverse-DNS plugin id deliberately before first Portal publish; it can never be reassigned.
Declare hard version floors as numbers: Kotlin-DSL plugin on Gradle 9.x needs consumer Gradle >=8.11, Groovy-DSL >=7.0, minimum KGP 2.0.0.
Read ocx --format json env via a ValueSource with injected ExecOperations (config-cache-exempt), never via raw System.getenv()/ProcessBuilder at configuration time.

Hold the parsed env result in a BuildService for the rest of the build; the dependency direction is ValueSource -> value -> BuildService, never BuildService driving a ValueSource (documented unsupported).
surprises: validatePlugins presence is a red herring for "does this repo publish a plugin" — 10/32 corpus repos run it purely for internal build-logic convention modules via java-gradle-plugin, with zero Portal signal (nowinandroid, sqldelight).

Gradle explicitly documents that a BuildServiceProvider cannot drive a ValueSource's parameters at configuration time — this fixes the ValueSource-vs-BuildService seat question as a one-way dependency, not a stylistic choice.

The three afterEvaluate replacements aren't three interchangeable options — they map to three distinct problems (deferred reads, optional defaults, cross-plugin reaction), and the docs name exactly one narrow carve-out (fail-fast validation of your own plugin's state, last-registered-only).

Settings plugins carry a hidden structural cost: folding one into a shared build-logic composite build forces pluginManagement{} inclusion, which reduces build-cache capability — Gradle's own fix is a separate minimal build-logic-settings build, confirmed only in gradle/gradle itself in the corpus checked.

ExecOperations.exec accepts an explicit environment(map) that replaces rather than extends the ambient environment, giving Gradle a native primitive for OCX's site/translucent/explicit/pinned classification even though Gradle has no built-in classification scheme of its own.

Two Gradle-10-scheduled removals are plugin-author-specific and easy to miss: Project.getProperties() and Project.container(...), both still legal in 9.x but silently breaking on the next major upgrade.

top_rules: A plugin's version-support claim MUST be tested with GradleRunner.withGradleVersion(...) across 3 legs: declared floor, current stable, and release-candidate — 2-leg 'current only' matrices are inadequate.
A configuration-cache functional-test leg MUST run separately from the version matrix — CC and version compatibility are orthogonal failure modes.

A plugin declaring compileOnly on another plugin's API MUST NOT use GradleRunner.withPluginClasspath() in functional tests; publish to a local Maven repo and consume it via the test's settings.gradle(.kts) instead — the failure mode is a misleading ClassNotFoundException, not a compile error.
TestKit functional tests MUST NOT assert on in-process state — TestKit runs the build in a separate process via the Tooling API with its own daemons and classloaders.

CI MUST run './gradlew publishPlugins --validate-only' on every change and read GRADLE_PUBLISH_KEY/SECRET from env vars, never committed properties, in the gated release job that runs bare publishPlugins.
validatePlugins { enableStricterValidation = true } MUST be set on any module that applies com.gradle.plugin-publish — the default only checks the plugin's own task types, not exported types.

validatePlugins task presence MUST NOT be used as a signal that a module publishes to the Portal (java-gradle-plugin registers it for any convention-plugin module too, 10/32 exemplar files); route on com.gradle.plugin-publish presence instead.

A published gradlePlugin{} block MUST set website, vcsUrl, per-plugin id/implementationClass/displayName/description/tags, and (plugin-publish 2.1.0+, March 2026) a compatibility { features { configurationCache = true } } declaration — currently a warning if absent, with a stated but undated plan to become a hard rejection.

Applying com.gradleup.shadow to a plugin is the sanctioned auto-wired shading path (since plugin-publish 1.0.0) — but treat relocation as a separate, narrower decision required only for dependencies at genuine risk of colliding in a shared, non-isolated classloader, not as an automatic consequence of shading.
org.gradle.testkit.dir / withTestKitDir(...) MUST be pinned to a project-relative, clean-swept location on any long-lived CI runner, since TestKit's default working directories are not deleted.
surprises: com.gradle.plugin-publish 2.1.0 (dated to the March 2026 Gradle newsletter) auto-applies a whole separate plugin (gradle/gradle-plugin-compatibility-plugin) that makes a Configuration-Cache compatibility declaration deprecated-if-absent, with a stated intent to eventually hard-reject undeclared plugins — no cutover date announced yet.

Shadow's own build does not shade or relocate itself despite being the shading tool, because Gradle isolates each plugins{ id(...) } plugin into its own classloader by default — the 'shade a plugin, therefore relocate everything' generalization is wrong; the mandatory-relocation case (error-prone in javac) is specifically about a shared, non-isolated classloader.

validatePlugins running in a build tells you almost nothing about Portal publishing on its own — 10/32 exemplar files hit the task purely because java-gradle-plugin registers it for internal convention-plugin modules, with 7 of those repos showing zero other Portal signal.

detekt runs a genuinely separate compilation (not just a different GradleRunner call) pinned to its floor Gradle version via a dedicated resolvable configuration and PluginUnderTestMetadata task, which is a stronger floor-proof than a single withGradleVersion() call.

Shadow's functional-test target needs four explicit --add-opens JVM args to test configuration-cache behavior via GradleRunner.withDebug(), an operational wrinkle tied to a 2022 Gradle issue whose continued necessity on the current JDK 17 floor is unverified.

Two incompatible gradlePlugin{ plugins{} } id-declaration idioms (create("id"){} map-key vs explicit id="...") remain in live, current use with no winner — Shadow and detekt use different but equally current syntax.

conflicts_resolved: A — Topic map conflict 1 claims `com.gradle.plugin-publish` auto-applies `com.gradleup.shadow`; the primary doc and `GradleUp__shadow@541b3be475:build.gradle.kts` (applies plugin-publish, neither shades nor relocates itself) show it only auto-publishes the shadow jar IF Shadow is applied. Resolved toward the dive: shading a plugin is opt-in and SHOULD, not the sanctioned default — the map's phrasing is corrected.

B — testkit dive demands three MUST TestKit legs (floor/current/release-candidate); detekt, the sharpest plugin-as-product exemplar, runs two, and the RC leg exists only in gradle/actions (an Action, not a plugin). Resolved by splitting severity: floor + current MUST (GRADLE-PLUG-12), release-candidate SHOULD and scheduled-only (GRADLE-PLUG-13) — an RC break is an upstream regression and a red PR trains people to ignore the matrix.

C — config-inventory Axis 4 left the seat for the `ocx --format json env` read open between ValueSource, BuildService and Provider. Resolved one way only on a documented impossibility ('a BuildServiceProvider cannot drive a ValueSource at configuration time'): ValueSource reads, BuildService holds the parsed value; recomputing per task is rejected for multiplying spawns and reopening the ambient-env hole.

D — testkit dive calls `enableStricterValidation` a MUST; gates audit measures 1/32 adoption (detekt only). Resolved toward the dive with scope narrowed to modules applying `com.gradle.plugin-publish`: the mechanism decides it — stricter mode is the only check covering the plugin's EXPORTED types, whose failures land in consumers' builds. Flagged as a new commitment and as owner question Q3.

E — `validatePlugins` presence reads as a 'this repo ships a plugin' signal; pub audit measured 10/32 files across 7 repos, 7 of them with zero Portal signal (nowinandroid, sqldelight). Resolved: route on `com.gradle.plugin-publish` (GRADLE-PLUG-20) — this is what keeps the Portal rows off the OCX SDK's own build-logic modules.

F — M-F-07 / map conflict 5 leaves the `gradlePlugin { plugins { } }` id idiom split. Shape audit: map-key form dominant where the plugin IS the product (shadow, detekt), explicit `id = "…"` dominant in spring-boot. Resolved: neither is wrong — write the map-key form in new code; an idiom-only rewrite is churn, demoted from a rule to failure mode 11.

Does a plugin whose public API is consumed from a Kotlin DSL build script need JSpecify annotations, given Kotlin treats JSpecify as `strict` (errors) and JSR-305 as `warn` — i.e. does keeping JSR-305 on a plugin API break consumer build scripts under Kotlin 2.2/K2, or only warn?

top_rules: A dependency whose type appears in a public superclass/interface, public method signature, public field, or public annotation MUST be `api`; everything else MUST be `implementation` — verify with `./gradlew :module:projectHealth`, not `compileJava`, since the failure surfaces at the consumer's build.

A published library MUST NOT use `enforcedPlatform()` — it overrides even a consumer's own explicit version, and Gradle's own docs single out this exact caution for reusable components; spring-boot@93b23c40c2 (13 hits) is the corpus's negative exemplar.
`enforcedPlatform()` is acceptable only in a leaf application module with zero library/plugin consumers of its own — never in anything `api`-published.

A library's own declarations MUST NOT use `strictly`/`!!` — it acts like a forced version for every consumer and is lossy when published (POM keeps only the strongest declaration; `reject` vanishes entirely).

A version catalog entry pins the DECLARED request only, never the RESOLVED version — Gradle's own docs state conflict resolution can still pick something else with no build failure and no diff in the catalog.

Never conclude 'no catalog' from a `**/gradle/libs.versions.toml` filename glob alone — grep `versionCatalogs\s*{` in settings files instead; apollo-kotlin@c145295b72 names its catalog `gradle/libraries.toml`, and gradle/gradle itself wires three named catalogs programmatically.
'Versions are pinned' requires a catalog PLUS either a checked-in lockfile or a platform/BOM constraint participating in resolution — a catalog alone is not pinning (0/32 exemplars lock at all).

`fixDependencies --upgrade` is the only safe unattended auto-fix mode because it never removes or downgrades a declaration, only adds/upgrades (e.g. implementation→api) — unrestricted `fixDependencies` can break a consumer relying on a leaked transitive type.
surprises: gradle/gradle — the tool that invented version catalogs — does not use the conventional `gradle/libs.versions.toml` path for its own build at all; it wires three named catalogs (libs/testLibs/buildLibs) programmatically, a blind spot for any filename-only glob rule.

spring-boot, a library, is the corpus's ONLY enforcedPlatform() user (13 hits) — the exact anti-pattern Gradle's own docs warn a reusable component against, shipped by one of the most widely-depended-on Java libraries in existence.

0/32 exemplars use dependency locking at all, so 'version catalog' and 'pinned versions' are conflated everywhere in practice even though Gradle's own docs explicitly distinguish declared vs resolved.

No wave-1 audit or this dive could confirm any of the 32 exemplars actually apply DAGP (`com.autonomousapps.dependency-analysis`) to themselves — the tool this brief centers on is undermeasured in the very corpus used to justify it.

DAGP's own README is AsciiDoc, not Markdown, and its FAQ wiki page does not define the four advice categories (unused/wrong-configuration/transitive/annotation-processor) at all — those live only on the wiki's Home page, a routing trap for anyone fetching just the README or just the FAQ as the brief's phrasing implies.

top_rules: OCX SDK/plugin builds MUST enable dependencyLocking with a committed gradle.lockfile per project — 0/32 exemplars do this, so it's a new commitment not a codified convention
Never combine dependency locking with -SNAPSHOT/changing versions in the same configuration — Gradle's own docs call this a misunderstanding that produces unpredictable results
CI must never run --write-locks in the same job as the main build/release, since a failed build silently drops lock-state changes

An SDK/plugin build MUST bootstrap gradle/verification-metadata.xml (sha256,pgp) AND require a second reviewer on every diff to that file — the bootstrap trusts whatever's currently resolvable, the reviewed diff is the actual control
verification-metadata.xml must rely only on sha256/sha512 entries; md5/sha1 alone is not verification per Gradle's own docs
PGP verification MUST maintain an explicit <trusted-keys> allowlist by full 40-char fingerprint — a valid signature only proves signing, never signer legitimacy

Internal group coordinates MUST use exclusiveContent{filter{includeGroup()}}, not bare content{}, given the Jackson org./com. prefix-swap attack passed Central's own domain-exact namespace verification

An agent proposing any dependency version bump MUST run a live resolution (./gradlew <module>:dependencies --write-locks/--refresh-dependencies) and refuse to emit any version it did not observe actually resolve — Sonatype measured ~28% (up to 1-in-4 for older models) of unvalidated LLM version recommendations as nonexistent
surprises: The one gradle.lockfile hit in the entire 32-repo corpus is gradle/gradle's own documentation snippet demonstrating the feature to readers, not a real lock on any build — locking has zero genuine exemplar support anywhere in the corpus.

Maven Central's namespace verification is what let the Jackson prefix-swap attack (org.fasterxml.jackson.core vs real com.fasterxml.jackson.core) through legitimately: DNS verification is domain-exact, so the attacker registering fasterxml.org passed verification for the org. namespace on its own merits — verification worked correctly and was still the wrong control.
Only gradle/gradle itself (1/32) has verification-metadata.xml among 32 flagship JVM exemplars including major libraries like okhttp, guava, and jackson-databind.

Sonatype's actual per-model hallucination rates span 7%-25%+ depending on generation (older models ~1-in-4, 2026 frontier models ~7-8%) — the brief's flat '28%' is the upper/older-model end, not a single stable figure, and is dropping fast.

Gradle's own docs state the bootstrap command's trust limitation in almost the exact words a security review would use ('trusts whatever is currently in your repositories'), making 'run the bootstrap command' insufficient as a rule on its own — it needs a mandatory reviewed-diff step attached.
A failed Gradle build silently discards any --write-locks changes, so a naive CI script chaining --write-locks with the main build can mask lockfile drift as if nothing happened.

top_rules: Bind maven-enforcer-plugin with an explicit <execution><goal>enforce</goal>; the plugin runs zero rules until bound (default lifecycle phase is `validate`).
Bind dependencyConvergence at ERROR on multi-module reactors with shared transitive libraries — mediation has no floor check of its own.
Bind banDuplicatePomDependencyVersions at ERROR everywhere; it costs nothing to configure and 0/32 corpus exemplars use it.
Bind banDynamicVersions at ERROR (default all-false allow-flags) on anything released; grep for ranges/SNAPSHOT/LATEST/RELEASE as the fast local proxy.
Bind requireUpperBoundDeps at ERROR as the cheap universal floor check — grpc-java's 8 example poms already prove real-world adoption.
Bind requirePluginVersions (banLatest/banRelease/banSnapshots/banTimestamps all true) to mechanize what assertj and guava already do by hand in pluginManagement.
Never explain a resolved Maven version by mediation alone — check `mvn help:effective-pom` for a dependencyManagement entry first, since it wins before mediation is even consulted.

A Gradle-built, Maven-consumed POM (the OCX SDK) needs no Maven-specific mechanism beyond a fully-resolved, non-dynamic, complete POM — the one real risk is a version-catalog placeholder or SNAPSHOT leaking into a released coordinate.
surprises: Maven 4.0.0 is confirmed still RC as of 2026-09-12: Central's index tops out at maven-core 4.0.0-rc-6, with 3.9.16 the latest stable — bom packaging and consumer-POM flattening are migration-preview only, not adoptable yet.
grpc-java binds requireUpperBoundDeps in 8 examples/*/pom.xml files (enforcer 3.5.0) — a real, un-briefed adoption data point for that rule beyond assertj/guava.

The ASF parent POM (v39) enforces only Maven/Java version floors and a signed reproducible-release profile — zero dependency-drift protection, which falsifies the assumption that a strict widely-inherited parent already covers convergence/duplicate checks.

Maven's own docs flag that dependencyManagement can silently downgrade an unrelated dependency sharing coordinates — a documented footgun distinct from the mediation-vs-management confusion the brief anticipated.
Version range gotcha confirmed verbatim from primary docs: `[1.0,2.0)` includes `2.0-rc1` because '2.0-rc1' sorts below '2.0' — contrary to most users' expectation.

assertj and guava both pin every plugin version manually in pluginManagement but neither binds requirePluginVersions itself (0/32) — manual discipline with zero enforcer backstop is the norm, not the exception.

strictly/!! severity: declaration-and-catalogs proposed MUST but flagged its own grep as untested against the corpus and said it 'should be SHOULD until measured'. Resolved against declaration-and-catalogs: a platform constrains which versions are allowed for the coordinates it names and records nothing about what was resolved for the ones it does not, so it cannot detect drift. GRADLE-DEP-09's check is a committed lockfile, full stop.

Locking severity: locking-verification's own Contested section narrows its candidate-1 MUST to 'MUST for the OCX SDK and Gradle plugin, SHOULD elsewhere'. Adopted, because 0/32 exemplars lock — making it a blanket MUST would flag every repo in the corpus including gradle/gradle.

DAGP as a gate: declaration-and-catalogs recommended `issues { all { onAny { severity("fail") } } }` while flagging corpus adoption as entirely unmeasured (its Contested #1). Measured today: 2/32 — gradle/gradle fails only on duplicate-class warnings (gradlebuild.root-build.gradle.kts:25), detekt applies build-health 3.19.1 (settings.gradle.kts:54). dependencyConvergence vs requireUpperBoundDeps as the Maven default: maven-mediation-and-enforcer explicitly left both open (its Contested #1). Resolved: `requireUpperBoundDeps` is the universal floor (cheaper, fewer false positives in a large reactor, real adoption base in grpc-java's 8 example POMs) and `dependencyConvergence` is added only where two or more paths genuinely reach the same library (assertj's shape, 1/32).

top_rules: Never shade a consumable library — shading is only for CLIs, javac/annotation-processor plugins, and Gradle plugins (zero counterexamples in 32 exemplars)

Every shaded jar merging 2+ dependencies' META-INF/services/* MUST call mergeServiceFiles() (Gradle) or configure ServicesResourceTransformer (Maven) — the default duplicate strategy silently drops providers
Bundling log4j-core requires Log4j2PluginsCacheFileTransformer — it's a binary cache file, not merged by mergeServiceFiles() or plain concatenation

Spring's spring.factories has NO built-in Shadow transformer as of 2026-09-12 (GradleUp/shadow#1489, open since 2025-06-26) — AppendingTransformer corrupts its keyed-Properties merge; only spring/*.imports (line-list) is safely handled by mergeServiceFiles()

Every shaded jar MUST exclude META-INF/*.SF, *.DSA, *.RSA, and *.EC — re-signing the output does not fix the signed-jar SecurityException because the original signature is now over content that no longer matches

Multi-release-jar module-info.class leakage is excluded by default only on Shadow >= 9.0.0 (2025-08-07, shadow#1177/#729) — builds below that floor must exclude META-INF/versions/*/module-info.class manually

Split packages across two shaded libraries have NO fix via any transformer — JEP 261's split-package prohibition means the only real fix is relocating one side's package before shading; verify by diffing package sets across the two dependency jars

minimize() is unsafe unless every reflection/ServiceLoader-using dependency is explicitly excluded via minimize{exclude(dependency(...))} AND CI runs the shaded jar's own functional tests — its one documented blind spot (Class.forName(String)) is exactly how ServiceLoader works internally
surprises: google/error-prone does NOT relocate packages when shading, contradicting the wave-1 topic map's conflict-1 claim — its core/pom.xml maven-shade-plugin execution only restricts artifactSet includes, with createDependencyReducedPom=false and no <relocations> block at all; the one <relocation> grep-hit in the repo is an unrelated distributionManagement artifact-move notice in type_annotations/pom.xml

Maven Shade's dependency-reduced POM defaults to true and is required only when the shaded jar publishes under normal (non-classified) coordinates; error-prone explicitly sets it to false because it ships a classified with-dependencies jar alongside an unshaded primary artifact — a real, code-backed answer to the brief's decision (c)
jmh-gradle-plugin's own current upstream fix for the signed-jar SecurityException omits .EC (ECDSA signature files) from its exclude list — the most commonly copy-pasted reference fix has this gap

grpc-java's and dagger's preserveFileTimestamps grep hits are confirmed (via the pub audit) to be a hand-written Transformer method parameter name, not the Gradle archive property — a durable grep trap worth naming explicitly in the depth file

Shadow has no built-in transformer for Spring's spring.factories as of today (GradleUp/shadow#1489 still open) even though the shape of the fix is well understood by the maintainers and multiple third parties have hand-rolled SpringFileTransformer implementations

No exemplar in the 32-repo corpus was found actually using minimize() at all — the caution around it is sourced entirely from Shadow's own docs and issue history, not corroborated (or contradicted) by real exemplar usage

top_rules: A jar declared as a dependency and consumed via its API MUST NOT be shaded — zero counterexamples in 32 exemplars
Classify the artifact first: (a) program, (b) plugin/agent host-loaded, or (c) API dependency — the shape is a lookup on that answer, not a preference
Default a general JVM application to the `application` Gradle plugin baseline unless a more specific shape's precondition holds
Spring Boot apps MUST use nested `bootJar`, never shading — none of the merge-failure taxonomy can occur since nothing merges
Layered-jar `layerOrder` MUST stay `dependencies, spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies, application` — reordering defeats Docker cache reuse on every commit
`jlink` MUST NOT run against a module graph containing an automatic module — it hard-fails; fix is exclude-to-classpath or find a modularized replacement
`jpackage` builds are per-OS only, and a macOS build MUST run notarization as a separate step after `jpackage` — signing alone isn't enough
Never `COPY` a single fat/shaded jar into a Dockerfile — use Jib or separate dependency/application COPY layers, or shading's lack of internal layering collapses Docker's cache too
surprises: The YouTrack SUPPORT-A-2700 article body is a client-rendered SPA that couldn't be scraped via WebFetch or curl — had to corroborate its content via an independent tacosteemers.com walkthrough and cite YouTrack as topic-only confirmation
jpackage has macOS signing flags but genuinely no notarization step of its own per the official spec — notarization is always a separate xcrun notarytool invocation, worth its own MUST

Jib's own layer split (other deps → snapshot deps → project deps → resources → classes → extra dirs) is finer-grained than Spring Boot's 4-layer order but follows the identical stable-to-volatile principle

Application-plugin usage (7/32) and Spring Boot's 383 bootJar hits both skew hard to sample/smoke-test modules, not shipped executables — citing either raw count without the per-module caveat would mislead
JEP 493 (jlink without JMODs) is a JDK-vendor opt-in build flag, not a universal JDK 24+ guarantee — no cross-linking, and an image built this way can't itself include jdk.jlink

0/32 exemplars use jlink or jpackage at all, so those two sections are precondition-derived from primary docs rather than corpus-corroborated — flagged explicitly in the file rather than presented as measured practice

GRADLE-DIST-04 — A library SDK ships exactly the library jar, sources jar, javadoc/Dokka jar and a complete POM/GMM — no application, bootJar, jlink, jpackage or container output. [MUST]

top_rules: Wire Error Prone + NullAway at the compiler-plugin layer on every Java module (net.ltgt.errorprone/net.ltgt.nullaway in Gradle; maven-compiler-plugin annotationProcessorPaths in Maven) — the only gate that runs on every compile.
Use OnlyNullMarked=true (NullAway 0.12.3+), not AnnotatedPackages, for new modules — package-prefix lists rot as code moves.
Never set both AnnotatedPackages and OnlyNullMarked, and never neither — NullAway fails the build immediately either way.
Before jspecifyMode=true, verify JDK 22+, or 17.0.19+/21.0.8+ on OpenJDK (not Oracle) with -XDaddTypeAnnotationsToSymbol=true — otherwise IllegalStateException at compile time.

Promote DefaultLocale, StringCaseLocaleUsage (severity bump only — it's already ENABLED_WARNINGS), EqualsMissingNullable, FieldMissingNullable, VoidMissingNullable, CatchingUnchecked, UnusedException, ConstantPatternCompile, UnnecessaryDefaultInEnumSwitch to ERROR on every new module.
Never rethrow a caught exception without passing it as cause — enforce via -Xep:UnusedException:ERROR.

Pick one Checkstyle base (google_checks.xml recommended) and commit a pruned copy — the two shipped rulesets diverge on more than half their modules, so shipping either unmodified misrepresents real practice.
Do not add PMD to a new JVM project's gate — 0/32 flagship exemplars enforce it; Error Prone + NullAway + find-sec-bugs cover its unique value better.
SpotBugs earns a place only bundled with find-sec-bugs (spotbugsPlugins com.h3xstream.findsecbugs:findsecbugs-plugin:1.14.0), and only on modules parsing untrusted input.

Adding a new overload is binary-*compatible* by JLS (old binaries keep resolving to the old signature) even though it can silently redirect which overload *new* source compilations pick — a source-compat, not binary-compat, hazard that cuts the opposite way from intuition

top_rules: Enable explicitApi() strict mode on every published Kotlin module — a missing visibility/type becomes a compiler error, not a lint warning
Never expose a data class in a published public API — one property addition changes both the constructor and copy() descriptors

Adopt the standalone binary-compatibility-validator plugin, not abiValidation{}, for a greenfield library today — abiValidation requires @OptIn(ExperimentalAbiValidation::class) and has 0/32 corpus adoption vs 5/32 for the standalone plugin
Never rely on @JvmOverloads alone for binary compatibility on a new default parameter — it only generates Java-visible overloads; Kotlin callers still hit NoSuchMethodError
Treat every @PublishedApi internal declaration under the same binary-compat review as public — its body is inlined into every caller of the public inline function
Never take a bare Boolean parameter in a public constructor or top-level function — split into named functions or an enum class
Propagate @RequiresOptIn markers through every public signature that uses the marked type — opt-in does not propagate automatically
Never reuse @RequiresOptIn to deprecate an already-shipped stable declaration — use @Deprecated(message, replaceWith, level) walking WARNING to ERROR to HIDDEN to removal instead
KDoc every public member except non-documenting overrides, but verify it via Dokka's report, not the compiler — unlike the visibility/type rules this one has no compile-time gate
An adopter already on the standalone BCV plugin should NOT migrate to abiValidation{} yet — it remains Experimental with zero corpus adoption and no compatibility guarantee
surprises: Narrowing a return type breaks binary compatibility exactly like widening does — it looks source-safe (even type-safe) and still throws NoSuchMethodError because the JVM call site is bound to the exact erased descriptor
Adding a value to an annotation's @Target set can silently redirect Java-reflection lookups from a field to the compiler-preferred property target, with zero Kotlin-side symptom and no compile error

@JvmOverloads is Java-callers-only and does nothing for Kotlin callers — the only mechanism that fixes both (@IntroducedAt under ExperimentalVersionOverloading) is itself still Experimental, so there is no fully-solved, stable answer to 'add a default parameter without breaking Kotlin callers' today
